item.title: No revival in sight for 'fragile' Spurs after Villa defeat
item.description: Tottenham look no closer to solving their problems as they slip to a home defeat by Aston Villa to add to their Premier League misery.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

It was all so predictable.

The closer Tottenham went to scoring the more it seemed likely they would concede.

"Too fragile" was how boss Roberto de Zerbi described his side after the 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa.

Comfortable and on top until Johan Manzambi's scrappy opener for the visitors - while Spurs were temporarily down to 10 men as Micky van de Ven had treatment - they never recovered.

It only got worse as goals from Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendia put the visitors 3-0 up.

De Zerbi's men now go into a three-week international break still waiting for a first Premier League win this season as Conor Gallagher and Jan Paul van Hecke's late goals - the club's first in the league - were of little consolation.

In the bottom three after spending over £300m in the summer there appears to be no end in sight to Spurs' struggles.

Tottenham have failed to win any of their last 36 Premier League matches when conceding first so the writing was on the wall at half-time.

They dominated the opening 20 minutes and Villa keeper Zion Suzuki denied Savio and Archie Gray but, without a goal, they were always going to be vulnerable at the other end.

And so, in first-half injury time, a Villa goal was almost inevitable.

Andy Robertson tried to stop a corner but only gifted the ball to John McGinn and, after Boubacar Kamara's effort, Manzambi prodded in from close range. It added the insult to Van de Ven's injury, a blow to the face that kept him off the pitch.

Some Tottenham fans missed the goal as they headed for their half-time refreshments but several thousand did not bother to stay until the end.

They streamed out of the stands after Buendia's brilliant 25-yard bullet found the top corner in the 79th minute, missing Gallagher and Van Hecke's late efforts.

De Zerbi said: "My focus is why we concede the first goal with 10 players, we can stay stronger, communicate more and more, defend in a compact way.

"I put [Rodrigo] Bentancur as a centre-back in that minute and Mateus Fernandes as a midfielder. If we have a red card we can play 70 minutes with 10 players.

"In the second half we scored the goal with [Mohammed] Kudus, offside, I don't know if some players lost energy but we conceded an unacceptable goal. We knew this season Aston Villa are playing 86% more long balls than last season.

"We had many meetings [about it] and we have to explain another game like Newcastle where we played the first half well and then we lose. It's my responsibility.

"I take my responsibility but in that moment of the game we have to defend, we have to defend compact, the leaders have to be leaders.

"I am very sad and frustrated with the performance. We cannot lose this game in this way. The second goal we conceded was incredible."

"Sacked in the morning" chanted the Villa fans to De Zerbi who, at times, looked out of ideas once his side fell 2-0 behind.

It was Tottenham's worst start to a top-flight season since 2008-09, when they also had two points after five games.

Juande Ramos was dismissed as manager after three more defeats before Harry Redknapp lifted them up to eighth. Spurs have also now gone five league games without a win at the start of a season for the first time since 1986.

Former Brighton striker Glenn Murray, however, says De Zerbi needs time.

"He is trying to build something, it will take time," he told BBC's Final Score. "Taking the emotion out of it, looking at the stats, they have had more shots in three of the past four games, more possession and more touches in the opposition box.

"They are positives, be patient, the metrics are there to say he will turn it around. They need to be patient with Roberto De Zerbi, with all the signings, it takes time to gel and get to know each other."

A decisive moment came when Kudus thought he had levelled on the hour, but Robertson was ruled just offside having delivered the cross. Seven minutes later Jackson scored from Suzuki's long launch downfield and it was game over.

Villa's rebuild, the club committing to spending more than £250m was out of necessity because of their own high-profile exits.

There was an expectation change was forthcoming and the Europa League winners were always going to go through a period of transition.

But a first league victory was vital for them too after three defeats in their opening four games.

While Villa look in better shape as new players settle, Spurs have thrown money at their problems after two relegation battles, but are no closer to solving them.

Sandro Tonali, the £100m midfielder from Newcastle, was overshadowed by Villa's tenacious skipper McGinn - a £2.75m buy from Hibs eight years ago.

Brazil winger Savio was denied three times by the impressive Suzuki but faded, while Omar Marmoush was signed to bring goals, but provided nothing.

De Zerbi added: "I didn't speak with the players [afterwards], I didn't want to say anything. The players who go to the national team, they have to play and work.

"The others, [James] Maddison, Gallagher, [Dominic] Solanke, Tosin [Adarabioyo, [Marcos] Senesi, Savio have to work more because their physical condition, I didn't like in this game."

Spurs have overpaid for every player - Cole

Former Chelsea and England midfielder Joe Cole questioned Tottenham's transfer business after their spend of around £302m.

After Tonali, £85m went on bringing in Mateus Fernandes from West Ham. The Portuguese midfielder was subbed at half-time and De Zerbi said he "didn't like" Fernandes' performance, while £75m was spent on Savio from Manchester City.

Marmoush will cost £60m once his loan becomes permanent but Spurs need their big-money buys to prove their worth and perform sooner rather than later.

"Spurs are dominant, chances, and you felt the tension growing - all of a sudden Spurs were just wanting to get to half-time. Once you defend with anxiety, things happen," Cole told TNT.

"When these things go against you, they go against you, Van de Ven going off was a factor, they didn't deal with it well, when you are anxious you make rash decisions.

"Villa defended well but didn't deserve to go in a goal up, and then this place deflated.

"They are not picking up points, a club flirting with relegation two years in a row, I feel they have overpaid for every player they bought this summer - you can't rule them out from being in and around the relegation battle."

De Zerbi, though, defended their summer window despite their current malaise.

"I am happy with the squad but the market was long, the situation changed many times," he said.

"There was also financial fair play and we have to respect that. We didn't sell the players we thought there was a possibility to sell.

"The club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players. If we didn't make any different decisions it was because we couldn't."

item.title: Clark resigns as Hartlepool boss in post-match interview
item.description: Lee Clark resigns as Hartlepool United head coach after a sixth loss in seven games following the 3-1 home defeat by Worthing.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Lee Clark resigned as Hartlepool United head coach with immediate effect following their home defeat by Worthing.

The 3-1 loss was a third defeat in a row and a sixth in seven matches, pushing Pools down to 18th before the afternoon kick-offs in the National League.

Clark took over at Victoria Park in the summer after a short spell with Rotherham United at the end of last season, but fans called for his head during Saturday's game as Hartlepool's slump continued.

"I resign from my position with immediate effect," Clark, a former Newcastle, Sunderland and Fulham player, told BBC Radio Tees.

"I wanted to give this club and the fans something to be proud of, what they deserve, but I haven't been able to do that unfortunately."

The former Huddersfield Town and Birmingham City boss added: "I was excited to take the job and I wanted to be the man to get them back to where they need to be and deserve to be, but it hasn't worked out."

Pools were taken over in January by American businessman Landon Smith as the County Durham club aim to end their four-year stay in the National League.

But the search now begins for their ninth permanent manager or head coach in this period outside the English Football League.

item.title: Tudhope wins second Ayr Gold Cup on Pellitory
item.description: Pellitory wins the Ayr Gold Cup for trainer David O'Meara after a lengthy delay following heavy rain - a second victory in the race for jockey Danny Tudhope.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Pellitory won the Ayr Gold Cup for trainer David O'Meara after a lengthy delay following heavy rain overnight and on Saturday morning.

There were two inspections of the course, with races pushed back but ultimately cleared to go ahead.

Jockey Danny Tudhope, who became the first Scottish winner of this race in 50 years when he rode Summerghand to victory in 2022, took the glory again as he fended off Tuco Salamanca who finished in second, with joint-favourites Binhareer and Far Above Dream not placing.

Pellitory - owned by Evan Sutherland - is better known over seven furlongs, but that served him well over heavy ground, securing a first win over the shorter distance.

"He's never really been brought back to six furlongs, it was a bold move," Tudhope said.

"To win this race once was unbelievable, to win it twice is amazing. I couldn't be happier."

O'Meara added: "We felt he would [love these conditions]. He stays seven [furlongs] and has run over a mile - that's a huge thing today.

"Today was all about Evan and his horse, I'm delighted for him."

item.title: Ratcliffe 'must go' says Man Utd Muslim fan group
item.description: The Manchester United Muslim Supporters Club says United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe "must go" after he spoke out against immigration and said the country was "on the slide".
item.content:encoded:
• Published

The Manchester United Muslim Supporters group says club co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe "must go" after he spoke out against immigration levels and said the country was "on the slide".

Billionaire Ratcliffe, who is one of Britain's richest people and founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, made the comments in an interview with the BBC on Saturday.

Ratcliffe said the UK was in decline because of a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He has previously apologised for "offending some people" with his language after saying the UK had been "colonised by immigrants".

At the time, in February, United responded by saying the club "prides itself" on being "inclusive", while BBC Sport cited a source familiar with the Glazer family as understanding the club's majority shareholders were "horrified" by his initial remarks and saw them as showing "disregard for their ownership".

"We condemned those comments then," said a statement of no confidence from Manchester United Muslim Supporters Club (MUMSC) in the club's ownership, issued on Saturday.

"He [Ratcliffe] subsequently apologised for his choice of language. We hoped a lesson had been learned. Clearly, it has not.

"This week, Sir Jim has again placed immigration and people receiving benefits at the centre of his explanation for Britain's problems, arguing that nobody is 'tough enough' to deal with either.

"We find these latest comments deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable."

Ratcliffe campaigned for a Leave vote in the 2016 European Union referendum and has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

He acquired a 27.7% stake in Man Utd in 2024, and has since restructured the organisation, overseeing 450 redundancies, overhauling senior management and sacking two managers.

MUMSC highlighted that United's "players, staff, stewards, security teams and supporters come from different countries, cultures, ethnicities, religions and backgrounds".

The group added: "Manchester United would not be Manchester United without them. That diversity isn't a weakness of Manchester United. It is part of Manchester United."

In the statement, the MUMSC also called on the Glazer family to go.

MUMSC said its members were among the club's fans who hoped Ratcliffe's arrival "would finally signal meaningful change" after the Glazer family had "presided over Manchester United's decline".

However, the group pointed to "higher ticket prices" and "a stadium allowed to deteriorate", along with "a football team that continues to fall further behind where Manchester United should be", among their concerns which "now extend beyond the pitch".

Manchester United entered the weekend sitting 13th in the Premier League after gaining four points from their first four Premier League games, and they were knocked out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday with a 3-2 home defeat by Brighton.

"After years of decline, broken promises and repeated failure, Manchester United Muslim Supporters' Club has lost confidence in the current ownership structure of Manchester United Football Club," MUMSC concluded.

"Enough is enough. It is time for change. The Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe must go."

item.title: Ingebrigtsen pipped to 5km road gold in Copenhagen
item.description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen is pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Jakob Ingebrigtsen was pipped to victory in the men's 5km in a thrilling finish at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.

African 5,000m champion Dawit Seare found a reserve of energy to pip the Norwegian great and take gold for Eritrea, with compatriot Saymon Amanuel winning bronze.

Ingebrigtsen, 26, was taking part in only his sixth race of an injury-hit season, eight days after he won the 5,000m on the track at the Ultimate Athletics Championships in Budapest.

The Olympic 5,000m champion looked well out of contention until about the final kilometre but powered through to lead, until Seare caught and passed him in the dying stages to win in 12 minutes and 56 seconds.

Likina Amebaw of Ethiopia dominated the women's 5km, just six days after winning $150,000 (£112,000) for victory in the 5,000m in Budapest.

Amebaw was imperious, making an early break to win in decisive fashion in 14:41.

Caroline Gitonga of Kenya was seven seconds behind in second place and Rose Davies of Australia won bronze as Britain's Hannah Nuttall (15:08) came home in 10th.

Robert Farken of Germany was a surprise winner of the men's mile.

American Yared Nuguse led from the gun but was caught in the final 100m as Farken won in 3:51.80 for his first major title.

Jake Heyward of Britain was 11th in a personal best on the roads of 3:55.76.

Agathe Guillemot of France won the women's mile in 4:22.74, the fastest time in the world this year on the road, after timing her attack to perfection to beat Freweyni Hailu of Ethiopia.

Kenyan Mirriam Cherop was third with Katie Snowden of Great Britain 16th.

The half-marathon titles will be decided on Sunday, with the elite races forming part of a two-day festival of running in the Danish capital.

item.title: Manzambi catches eye as Villa beat Spurs - player ratings
item.description: Tottenham are still looking for their first Premier League goal of the season.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Aston Villa piled more misery on Tottenham with a comfortable win.

Johan Manzambi, Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendia struck as Villa earned their first league victory of the season.

Conor Gallagher and Jan Paul van Hecke scored late for Spurs but it was not enough.

Here's how BBC Sport rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.

Tottenham

Antonin Kinsky: Made a comfortable save from Manzambi's strike before a better one thwarted Buendia. There was little he could do to stop the goals. 6

Pedro Porro: Back after missing the draws against Nottingham Forest and Everton but his returned lasted 18 minutes as he limped off injured. Had made a positive start. 6

Jan Paul van Hecke: It looked a robust performance as he handled the nuisance of Jackson when Villa did venture forward but he was beaten by Manzambi to the ball for the opener. Scored late consolation. 6

Micky van de Ven: Took a blow to the face just before the break and was off the pitch for treatment when Villa scored, which summed up Spurs' afternoon. 5

Andrew Robertson: Made a mistake in trying to keep the ball in, which eventually led to Villa's first. Thought he had atoned, only to be ruled offside in the build-up to Kudus' disallowed goal. 5

Sandro Tonali: One first-half strike whistled wide but it was another underwhelming outing for the £100m midfielder. 5

Rodrigo Bentancur: Enjoyed the battle in an occasionally congested midfield but his influenced waned as the game wore on. 5

Savio: The forward should have put Spurs ahead early and an excellent volley was kept out by Suzuki, but after a strong opening 25 minutes he failed to build. 5

Mateus Fernandes: Replaced at half-time as Tottenham chased the game, the former West Ham midfielder the victim of the circumstances. 6

Omar Marmoush: The Manchester City loanee was brought in to get the goals but it was a listless display once the game started to go away from Tottenham. 5

Dominic Solanke: The striker has not scored in the Premier League since March and could not find a telling touch again. There was little to suggest his drought would end. 5

Subs:

Archie Gray (on 18, Porro): Could have scored with his first touch but was denied by Suzuki. That was as good as it got. 6

Mohammed Kudus (on 46, Fernandes): Came on with Tottenham needing more attacking impetus and had a goal disallowed but was not able to spark. 5

James Maddison (on 66, Solanke): The substitute was unable to make an impact from the bench. 5

Lucas Bergvall (on 84, Bentancur).

Conor Gallagher (on 84, Tonali). Late consolation was his second goal in successive games.

Subs not used: Dubravka, Tosin, Senesi, Udogie.

Aston Villa

Zion Suzuki: Kept Villa level with saves from Savio and Archie Gray in the first half. A fine performance but his usually excellent distribution let him down. 8

Aaron Wan-Bissaka: The right-back has struggled to adapt quickly under Unai Emery. One slip almost cost Villa a goal and was little surprise he was withdrawn at half-time. 5

Tyrone Mings: Lost the ball several times as Villa played out from the back but rediscovered his composure after the break. 6

Victor Lindelof: Relatively untroubled in the second half after needing to be alert to Spurs' early threat. Once that died down, it was a comfortable afternoon. 7

Matteo Ruggeri: A full Premier League debut for the left-back but he did not look convincing as he tries to understand what is needed by Emery. 6

Joao Gomes: In his first Premier League appearance after his opening-weekend dismissal, the midfielder was solid and able to protect Villa's lead. 7

Boubacar Kamara: It was the midfielder's shot which fell into the path of Manzambi to score, and he was able to keep Villa moving. 7

John McGinn: His tenacity was rewarded as he seized on Roberton's error to help set up Manzambi's goal. A typically dynamic display. 7

Emi Buendia: The forward loves a goal at Tottenham and scored the pick of the bunch when he found the top corner from 25 yards to seal it. 7

Johan Manzambi: A goal and an assist on his full debut for Villa as he grew into the game after a slow start when Tottenham dominated. More will be expected once he settles in. 8

Nicolas Jackson: Isolated for long spells in the first half but got his goal in the second and was a nuisance. Had earlier forced Kinsky into a smartsave. 7

Subs

Matty Cash (on 46, Wan-Bissaka): The right-back returned from injury to help strengthen Villa's defence. 7

George Hemmings (on 72, Manzambi): Helped Villa to a comfortable win.

Ibrahim Mbaye (on 84, Kamara).

Ross Barkley (on 84, McGinn).

Unused subs: Wright, Bogarde, Abraham, Garnacho, Harwood-Bellis.

item.title: Why the Black Country derby means so much to Wolves and West Brom
item.description: Wolves and West Bromwich Albion meet for the first time in a Black Country derby for the first time in the league since May 2021.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Wolverhampton Wanderers v West Bromwich Albion. The Black Country derby. A fixture that goes back to the very dawn of English footballing time itself.

Now it's back as a league fixture for the first time in more than five years, and in front of fans at Molineux since 2012.

It was first contested as a league game in December 1888 - the very first season of the Football League - when Wolves won 2-1. However, Albion had already won their first two meetings, in 1886 and 1887, both in the FA Cup.

Since then, there have been so many derby memories, both magic and tragic at opposite ends of the emotional scale.

And, since the explosion of televised football, so many of those moments captured on video to be relived - or mentally erased depending on your allegiance - over and over again.

It's a fixture that the Black Country never stops talking about, the first the fans look for when the sides are in the same division.

And the pre-match banter begins earlier with every staging - and every look back at all those derby highlights from the past 40 years.

Steve Bull's first derby goal in 1989, a toothlessly grinning Iwan Roberts' Hawthorns hat-trick in 1996, George Ndah's double on the back of an inspired Keith Andrews performance in 2001 and two-goal Steven Fletcher's matchwinning efforts in May 2011 to help keep Mick McCarthy's side in the Premier League.

For Albion, there was Darren Bradley's 35-yard screamer in 1993, Bob Taylor's late Hawthorns clincher in 1995, Jordao's Molineux matchwinner in December 2001, the season when Albion pipped Wolves for promotion by three points, and Carlos Vela's injury-time equaliser in Roy Hodgson's first game in charge in 2011.

And then there was that famous 5-1.

February 2012. Wolves 1-5 Albion. A day when Peter Odemwingie netted a hat-trick and a slightly older Andrews rubbed it in by scoring against his old club.

Wolves were ripped apart and boss McCarthy lost his job the next day.

Sunday's game is the first chance since when a 'gold and black' Molineux crowd will have been there to see their team try to avenge that day of great gloating from the 'stars in stripes'.

Wolves, relegated at the end of that campaign, just as they were again in May, have since spent eight seasons in the top flight, to Albion's seven - but only once at the same time.

That was the post-Covid season of 2020-21, when both derbies were played behind closed doors - and the Baggies took four points out of a possible six off their neighbours, but still got relegated.

It all adds up to why this Sunday's meeting is so important.

The first chance to truly avenge that 5-1 embarrassment - Wolves' joint second-worst in a Black Country derby, bettered only by an 8-0 home defeat in 1894, way back in the latter days of Queen Victoria's reign.

The history of this fixture is important. So much so for Albion boss James Morrison that, on top of their usual training sessions, he has had his players in for extra pre-match preparation from one of the Baggies' club historians, who will have been able to chiefly inform his players that, in terms of the entire 138-year history of this fixture, it is very close - 55 Albion league wins to Wolves' 52.

But, in recent years, the Baggies hold sway.

Since the beginning of the new Millennium, there have been 18 league and cup derbies, of which Albion have won 10 and Wolves just four - but they did win the most recent meeting, the 2-0 victory in the FA Cup fourth round at The Hawthorns in January 2024.

That was an occasion scarred by the poor behaviour displayed by a minority of fans as play was halted for 38 minutes after police were assaulted, missiles were thrown and flares were set off.

It this week led to the two clubs sending out a joint statement highlighting the need to keep the rivalry friendly.

But Morrison himself has already added to the pre-match mind games by even hinting that he half-expects to still see Wolves striker Raul Jimenez out there on Sunday, despite boss Cesar Peixoto having ruled out the Mexican earlier this week with a knee injury.

"I'll believe it when I see it," said the Albion boss.

Peixoto has since assured the Albion camp that the injury is for real. "I don't play mind games," he told BBC Radio WM.

But always, in any derby game, all the talk counts for little when the game gets under way.

And, prior to his first taste of the fixture, Peixoto said he was well aware of what it means to the fans and had a message for his players.

"Play with passion but also with your head," he said. "I'm very competitive. I don't like to lose."

Much may depend on the mental approach of both teams.

Wolves, just three points adrift of Albion in the early Championship table and with a game in hand, have already tasted one derby this season - the 2-2 thriller with Birmingham City a fortnight ago, when they were forced to settle for a point after conceding a comical own goal.

But Jose Sa's mix-up with Jackson Tchatchoua is just the sort of thing that can happen in a derby game, when the atmosphere is white hot and tensions high.

And, although Albion boss Morrison is experiencing his first Black Country derby as a head coach, he played in five of them - including that 5-1 win.

"These are the games you want to be involved in," he said. "The outcome can be a real positive for the players and myself. You can cement a special place with performances in these games."

item.title: Postponement not an option as Kenya races to be ready for Afcon 2027
item.description: African football boss Patrice Motsepe wants a "heightened sense of urgency" from Afcon 2027 co-hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda as they face a race to be ready.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

African football boss Patrice Motsepe has called for a "heightened sense of urgency" from next year's Africa Cup of Nations co-hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

The tournament is set to return to East Africa for the first time in 51 years, with the opening match kicking off on 19 June and the final scheduled for 17 July.

Stadiums are supposed to be ready for testing in around three months' time, and Confederation of African Football (Caf) president Motsepe says there is little room for delay.

"Even though we've got nine months, we need to start using those stadiums in January next year to test them and to see what further improvements are required," he told BBC Sport Africa after inspecting preparations in Kenya on Friday.

Motsepe said there had been "very good progress" while also acknowledging that some facilities were still below the required level.

"We've got very high standards in terms of our expectations of the infrastructure, the facilities and the stadiums, the hotels, the roads, the football pitches where training takes place," the South African added.

"We require those facilities to be world class."

Despite delays in certain areas, Motsepe insisted: "There isn't the slightest consideration of a postponement.

"There should be no need because there's a deep amount of commitment."

Kenya to 'accelerate preparations'

Motsepe began his inspection visit for Afcon 2027 in Tanzania before touring Kenya, where he inspected two venues in Nairobi: Kasarani Stadium and the newly constructed 60,000-capacity Talanta Stadium.

BBC Sport Africa understands that one of the main areas of concern in Kenya is the Kasarani and its corresponding training facility.

The stadium is set to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, which Nairobi was awarded on Tuesday ahead of London and Rome.

When Caf conducted its previous inspection in mid-February, the local organisers were told that stadiums and their associated training facilities should be around 80% ready by August.

However, Kasarani has seen limited progress over the past seven months, with several areas still requiring attention.

One of the biggest challenges is the playing surface, which is yet to be laid. Work is also required on cabling for broadcast and television operations, floodlights and the stadiums' sky boxes.

Motsepe also pointed to the demands created by hosting hundreds of VIPs and heads of state, saying some stadium designs will need to be reconfigured.

"Security issues in relation to where the special guests, particularly the heads of state, will be seated requires a revision of the original plans," the 64-year-old explained.

Kenya's cabinet secretary for sports Salim Mvurya insisted preparations would be completed on time.

"I assure Caf and Kenyans we will accelerate the preparations for Afcon 2027," Mvurya said.

"We will conclude everything by December to be sure we can have test matches in the various facilities."

December is significant because Motsepe is due to return to the region for a final assessment visit in January.

Recent Caf tournaments have regularly been delayed from their original dates.

This year's Women's Africa Cup of Nations was played in July after the planned kick-off in March was postponed with just 12 days' notice.

The 2024 African Nations Championship - the former tournament for home-based players only - in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda was postponed from its intended February 2025 dates to August 2025 to ensure infrastructure and facilities were "at the levels necessary". That decision came 18 days before the tournament was due to start.

Meanwhile, the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast was moved to the early months of 2024 because of concerns about the rainy season.

Two years ago Motsepe's former deputy Veron Mosengo-Omba admitted that Caf faced a "scheduling nightmare" to fit its biennial tournaments into the crowded football calendar.

Some pundits claim that is part of the reasoning behind the decision to play the men's Afcon every four years after 2028.

Sporting legacy

Despite previous delays to tournaments and concerns over preparations in East Africa, Motsepe has made it clear the Afcon 2027 timetable will not be reconsidered.

"There's no plan B, there's no plan C," he said.

For Kenya, getting it right this time matters more because Afcon has become part of a bigger sporting project.

"One of the reasons why Kenya won the 2029 World Athletics Championship bid is because we are hosting Afcon. Therefore this is a legacy," Mvurya said.

"Sport is not just entertainment, it is livelihood, it is economic transformation.

"Therefore we are aware the opportunity to host Afcon will be key for our economic inspiration. Our tourism will be a big beneficiary.

"As government, we are confident we will host a successful Afcon."

The next three months are likely to be particularly crucial in making that promise a reality.

item.title: Wales deliver performance of serious promise
item.description: Wales have set themselves a new standard after clocking up a half-century of points in their WXV opener against South Africa.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Wales have set themselves a new standard after an impressive eight-try victory over South Africa in their WXV Global Series opener.

It was a score even the most optimistic of fans could not have predicted against a team who went into the match ranked 10th in the world, three places above Wales, but the 50-19 scoreboard shone bright under Cardiff's Friday night lights.

Sean Lynn's side have been dealt their share of criticism in recent years, and understandably so with a winless World Cup and three Six Nations wooden spoons.

But they were unrecognisable in the Welsh capital as players shook off the shackles of the past and delivered a performance of real promise.

The new-look backline attacked with flair, the forwards carried with intent and so many players stood tall, all under the watchful eye of British and Irish Lions Women's coach Jo Yapp.

Old and new faces impress

Lynn had included three uncapped players in his matchday 23 and while they looked every bit at home in the international arena, it was the mainstays who most impressed.

Former Wales and Lions centre Jonathan Davies described Sisilia Tuipulotu's two-try display as world class and it would be hard to disagree.

The tight-head prop looked back to her bulldozing best, while Georgia Evans had a superb game at lock. Each would have been a worthy recipient of player of the match, but the accolade went to co-captain fantastic Alex Callender, the flanker showing what a miss she had been during the Six Nations.

Keira Bevan was a constant threat playing out of position at fly-half, while Lisa Neumann had one of her best games in a Wales shirt while filling in at full-back.

As for the newbies, Lynn said Freya Bell was "outstanding" on her first Wales start, while former Cardiff City footballer Amy Williams showed the speed and strength which makes her a hugely exciting prospect on the wing.

Wales' new DNA

This was Lynn's third victory since taking over as Wales head coach last year and he said he could not be prouder.

"There have been some tough times, but you've got to have those adverse times," he said.

"This is just the start for us, this is going to be our new DNA.

"Those 23 players were aligned in everything, both sides of the ball, and they had that belief of how hard we worked in pre-season.

"The growth in our skill development has been the underpin of everything.

"Keira Bevan said to me, she's had 84 caps and that's the first time Wales have scored 50 points. That for me is up there."

Lynn's only disappointment was that there had not been more people in the Arm's Park to witness Wales beating the Springbok Women - a sentence you do not hear every day.

"I want more people coming next week to watch what this team is about. There is more to come," he said.

Backing it up

Wales face USA, who like South Africa are ranked above Wales, on Saturday, 26 September, also at Cardiff Arms Park, in their second outing of the new WXV campaign.

And while Wales will enjoy their deserved celebrations, co-captain Kate Williams is already talking about the importance of backing the performance up.

"After all of the tough times we have been through, as a team and Welsh rugby generally, we are going to keep working for the positive feeling to continue," she said.

"What we want out of this WXV Series is more wins.

"Today just proved that what we've been doing works and we'll be able to change our gameplan for USA next week."

Lynn will be waiting on the fitness of scrum-half Seren Lockwood after she failed to return to the pitch after a head injury assessment, but he could be boosted by the return of Carys Cox, who gives him another exciting option in the backline.

Until then, he and Wales will enjoy victory before the work starts again on Monday.

item.title: The man who would be king - the rise and fall of 'the next Prince Naseem'
item.description: Touted as the king to Naseem Hamed's prince, Daniel Teasdale's story is instead a cautionary tale.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

Boxer Daniel Teasdale was hailed as the heir to the legendary Prince Naseem Hamed, but his promise never materialised into fame, fortune and films.

"He's better than Naz at the same age," said trainer Brendan Ingle.

Hamed had won his first world title aged 21. Teasdale was still a teenager.

Ingle, from his gym in Sheffield, moulded the careers of a conveyor belt of world-beaters and title winners. He guided both of the fighters from childhood.

Before super-middleweight Teasdale's first professional bout, the Rotherham fighter had been featured in national newspapers, books and was being documented by photographers and film-makers.

He won a succession of national titles, establishing himself as the next contender to emerge from the Ingle gym.

Photographer Simon Roberts travelled to the Ingle gym in 1997 hoping to photograph Hamed.

"Brendan said 'don't worry about Naz, start photographing that kid in the corner. He's going to be bigger than Naz'. That was Daniel," Roberts said.

Roberts began to follow the young sensation, hoping to capture his rise on camera.

Filmmaker Stuart Mitchell had a similar brief.

"We were selling the documentary as 'who's the next Prince Naseem?'," says Mitchell.

He recalls Teasdale being the subject of similar headlines in national newspapers, and later accompanying him to an event gathering together the best British prospects from every sport for the new Millennium.

Attention on Ingle's latest protégé was more than just hype.

"He was like Oscar de la Hoya," recalls former stablemate Amer Khan.

"Teasdale was exceptional as a junior, he was stopping everyone."

Teasdale learnt both ballet and gymnastics to develop his footwork and skills in the ring and was seemingly set for stardom.

"I was very teachable, could talk, had the looks and could box," says Teasdale, who took up the sport aged six.

The bitterness of Hamed's split from trainer Ingle in 1998 has been well-documented, with both sides seemingly losing.

"Brendan lost the focus with the up-and-comers," Teasdale says.

He followed Naz in leaving the gym, linking up with one of its greatest exports, three-time world title challenger Herol 'Bomber' Graham.

The exit was said to have been spearheaded by Teasdale's father who "essentially gave up his career" to help his son fulfil his potential, Roberts says.

It was funded by a businessman with no prior experience in boxing, but a thirst to be part of Teasdale's rise to the top.

Teasdale remembers Graham's influence as "a breath of fresh air", but the presence of others was less helpful.

"People started to try and feed off Daniel," says Roberts.

"I photographed [Mike] Tyson and Lennox [Lewis], I have seen all of this stuff before."

'Everybody wanted a piece'

Mitchell was also filming future Olympic bronze medallist Darren Sutherland when he arrived at the Ingle gym from Ireland.

"Daniel was probably more talented than Darren, the trouble with Daniel was he was always being wooed," reveals Mitchell.

Teasdale's tag as the next Prince Naseem also hung heavy.

"I was like catnip for cats, everybody wanted a piece," Teasdale explains.

While the career of some talented prospects is carefully nurtured, Teasdale may not have been as well protected.

"To some extent Daniel was used because he was seen as a big potential and was a good scalp for somebody who wanted to get through the ranks," Roberts says.

Different trainers, managers and promoters followed, but Teasdale admits instability harmed his progress.

His debut had been a disaster - abandoned due to rioting in the crowd - while the following year he received death threats before a bout.

Despite undeniable talent, those early misfortunes could now be seen as an omen of what was to come.

After filming Teasdale across five years, Mitchell shelved his documentary when commissioners lost interest.

He too lost faith after a training session in Graham's garage.

"It felt very small and I didn't think this was going anywhere," he says bluntly.

Many have since raised doubts over whether the "pretty boy" was made for a career getting punched in the face.

"Everybody has a weakness and mine was women," Teasdale confesses.

"I lost the edge and my focus wasn't where it should be."

He walked away from the sport in 2005 after he was stopped in the first round of a light-heavyweight contest - his first professional defeat.

He returned in 2010 and reunited with Ingle, winning his one and only comeback fight.

"After that I just gave it up, I thought 'I'm not going to be second best to the first me," says Teasdale, whose professional career ended after just five fights over a seven-year period.

"At 27 I should have been a world champion defending my title."

Roberts continued to photograph Teasdale.

"There were a lot of unfortunate circumstances with him which meant he didn't fulfil his potential," Roberts says.

"There was a lot of bad advice and a lot of people wanting something from him, and not necessarily for the good."

Mitchell did some "soul searching" over his role in Teasdale's journey.

"There was so much clamour around him - then it just evaporated," he recalls.

"That must be very difficult to deal with when expectations are that you are going to be a successful and famous boxer."

Teasdale says "everything went up in the air" as a professional, in contrast to the stability of his early years.

Bad management played a part in not fulfilling his potential, but he admits "living for other people's dreams and ambitions."

Still, there are no regrets about how his career turned out.

"It's made me who I am," says Teasdale, now enjoying an altogether different career as a support worker.

"I'm doing the job that I love, it's not the profile that I was but it's all about being stable in your life."

item.title: From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary
item.description: From obscurity and near oblivion to Premier League and Europe - Brighton celebrate their 125th anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
• Published

It is Thursday, 9 November, 2023. Brighton manager Roberto de Zerbi is addressing his players in the Amsterdam Arena before their Europa League tie with Ajax.

"There's 3,000 Brighton fans in this stadium tonight," said the Italian. "But there's more than twice that number in the city who have travelled over. Remember that when you go on to that pitch."

A long-standing senior Brighton official was in the dressing room that day. A fan first and foremost, but someone who has spent almost three decades working for the club.

"It made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up," he said.

For some clubs, an encounter with Ajax is commonplace. Not Brighton.

"The royalty of European football," says the official. "From where we've come from, to be in that environment. It was a pinch-me moment."

Brighton won 2-0. It was the high point of the first European campaign in the club's history.

Ask Paul Samrah for his single most memorable moment as a Brighton fan and a very different answer comes back, which goes to the heart of why, as they celebrate their 125th birthday around the visit of Arsenal, the Seagulls are almost unique among English clubs.

August 2007. "After the years of campaigning, the days and nights I spent fighting for regime change and then for the stadium, the moment I heard we'd actually got planning permission, that our objectors had decided not to continue their fruitless efforts to stop the stadium," he explained.

"We'd won our battle."

The two stories highlight the before and after reality of Brighton & Hove Albion.

Formed in 1901, Brighton were a Southern League club for almost two decades before they were voted into the Football League. They had experienced only seven seasons in Division Two when they were promoted to the top flight for the first time in 1979.

For years, they were known outside Sussex chiefly for "And Smith must score..." - the BBC radio commentary, delivered by the late Peter Jones, at a critical point during the 1983 FA Cup final, late in extra time. It was the moment when Gordon Smith, clear on goal with a chance to earn Brighton their first major trophy, saw his shot saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Gary Bailey. United won the replay.

But in 1995, chairman Bill Archer sold Brighton's Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, because of escalating debts that there was no obvious way of paying. Fans were not consulted and no alternative stadium was put in place.

Brighton did not leave until 1997, although their final season at the Goldstone was only confirmed by the property company who owned the stadium, after the final game of the 1995-96 campaign, which had to be abandoned as thousands of furious fans spilled on to the pitch to demonstrate against the ownership. Both crossbars were snapped amid the tumult.

After two seasons playing 70 miles away at Gillingham, and with the idea of a new stadium in the Toad's Hole Valley area of Brighton a non-starter, the club returned to the city in 1999 and started playing at Withdean Stadium, most famous for being the home athletics track of Olympic middle distance gold medallist Steve Ovett.

That brings us back to De Zerbi's pre-match team-talk at Ajax.

Brighton had more than 7,000 fans in Amsterdam that night. When they moved into the Withdean, its capacity was only 6,000. The modern Brighton really is a totally different club to the one that existed before.

"After the 1983 FA Cup final, players were sold, there was no investment, the Goldstone was decaying and the crowds were dipping," said Samrah. "There was no communication between board and fans, directors came and went. There was no continuity, no leadership, no direction. We were just rudderless."

There are some notable figures in the Brighton story.

Former Football Association executive director David Davies got involved, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott overturned a rejected planning application for Brighton's current stadium in Falmer. Former chairman Dick Knight stabilised a club that in 1997 came within 27 minutes of being relegated out of the Football League.

Without that trio, and many more, it is quite possible Brighton would not exist.

The contemporary Brighton are different.

They began their second European campaign in the Norwegian city of Tromso last month, knowing the Conference League offers the chance of that elusive first trophy.

They play in a magnificent stadium, a short train journey from the city centre, with its new corporate areas, and, generally, inclusive family atmosphere. Their recruitment model, buying players in and selling them on for vast profits, is envied. The new Brighton just beat Manchester United at Old Trafford for the fifth time in six visits. Four games into their 10th consecutive Premier League campaign, they sit fifth.

The contemporary Brighton exist the way they do largely because of the vision and investment of Tony Bloom.

Born in Brighton, Bloom is a lifelong fan. His connection to the club is through his grandfather Harry, a former vice-chairman, and uncle Ray, a director.

Bloom, 56, is an entrepreneur. He made his money in finance and gambling, largely through the use of data. He became chairman in 2009, and masterminded the rise from League One and move into the American Express Stadium. Last season, Brighton's average attendance was more than 31,000.

In their 125-year history, Brighton have never had it so good.

"Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.

"The club has been on an unbelievable journey. We've got staff members and many fans who have done that journey. For those of us who weren't here 15 years ago, our responsibility is to ensure what's to come - and I think there's lots - is better than what's happened in the recent or long-distance past."

As for Bloom himself, he has reflected on Brighton's 125th birthday in the programme for the Arsenal game.

"Since 1901, this football club has been part of the fabric of our city and the broader county of Sussex," he said.

"It has connected generations of families and communities. Grandparents have brought their children and grandchildren to matches. Lifelong friendships have been forged on terraces, in stands and on away trips.

"Through good times and bad, Brighton & Hove Albion has provided so many of us with some of the most memorable moments of our lives.

"This club is in my blood. Some of my earliest and most cherished memories are wrapped up in the sights and sounds of the Goldstone.

"When I had the privilege of becoming owner and chairman, it was like being entrusted with something precious to safeguard and help develop for the future.

"Many of you reading these words will remember those difficult years. The loss of the Goldstone. The long journeys to Gillingham. The challenges of the Withdean era.

"What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear. This anniversary belongs as much to those supporters as anyone. Quite simply, without them, we would not be here today."

Whether they beat Arsenal or not, Brighton stands tall, for those who fought to preserve something they felt was special, and a man who had a vision - and finance - to build something better.
